full_text:
Interviewer:	I'll just start of telling you a little bit about what we're doing. Er, we're interviewing students across all engineering disciplines, and people who are going on placement and people who aren't going on placement, to find out how that impacts on their career decisions (OK) and we're looking ultimately at trying to increase the amount of women – that's not just who enter engineering, but to help keep them in engineering once they actually get there. So if I can get a bit of background information off you to begin with - what course was it that you're on?

Subject:	I'm on mechanical engineering.

Interviewer:	Right, OK are you doing the extended or the normal?

Subject:	Yeah, at the moment, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, what A levels did you do?

Subject:	Geography, biology and design tech.

Interviewer:	OK not the normal physics and maths then? What type of school did you go to?

Subject:	A normal

Interviewer:	Yeah, was it like an all girls or anything like that?

Subject:	No..

Interviewer:	OK. Have you got any work experience?

Subject:	Er, I've done a couple of summer jobs erm but for 3 years I was a gymnastics coach for (??) but nothing in terms of engineering (right, OK) I've done the odd week here and there.

Interviewer:	Right, OK – what do your parents do? Are they engineers or anything?

Subject:	No, my dad's a Financial Manager and my mum's a Nurse.

Interviewer:	OK, I'm just going to ask you then a bit about why and how you decided to do engineering. So, what do you think made you decide to go into engineering?

Subject:	Erm, I don't know. I wanted to join the air force and then applied to be a pilot (right) and I was too short and I thought well if you can't – if you can't fly them, why not learn how they work and how to design them or how to build them you know, and it ended up carrying on from that really.

Interviewer:	Right, OK, so in terms of things that influenced your decision, it was probably the type of job that you wanted to do, or that you weren't able to do – ended up leading you into it?

Subject:	Yeah, as a kid I always sort of played with technic lego and stuff like that. And my Design, Technology I enjoyed and I got good marks and – and it carried on from there really, along with a couple of other things.

Interviewer:	OK. Have you come straight from school to University?

Subject:	Yeah, I did a foundation year, here at [this university].

Interviewer:	OK, so what about things like your family and careers advice, anything like that? Did that help you or…

Subject:	Careers Advice was awful at the school.

Interviewer:	Was it?

Subject:	Yeah, there wasn't really a lot of that, and what there was it was like, oh well how do you fancy becoming – you know – a shop assistant or erm, or what was I told I should become? – a shop fitter, you know. Putting shelves up in a shop basically – that was about as much information they gave and it was awful. You saw a Careers Advice person for say maybe, for 20 minutes, once a year, and it was a waste of time. (yeah) A complete waste of time.

Interviewer:	Did you tell them what you wanted to do?

Subject:	Er, yeah.

Interviewer:	And what kind of reaction did that get?

Subject:	It was nothing really and…

Interviewer:	And what about your family, have they been supportive?

Subject:	Yeah, they're supportive of whatever I chose to do.

Interviewer:	Yeah? OK, did you know any engineers to talk to, to find out what it is all about?

Subject:	I have a very close family friend who is just a retired – retired chartered engineer (right) and he kind of gave us some advice, told us a lot about the fact that our course is a lot of mathematical stuff, and in the end you just put it into a computer and it's part of what – of what – a lot of what you do here is not what you do in industry. (Yeah) But, not an awful lot of people really, just the odd one or two.

Interviewer:	Yeah, but what your friend said didn't put you off at all? What are the sorts of things that appeal to you about doing engineering?

Subject:	Er, working on technical projects and I think the engineering side of things moves more into management as you progress. And I think project management and that kind of thing. Also, I'd always thought about being some sort of human factors – er, you know, the way people interact with machines or stuff – or ergonomics always interested me. It kind of opens doors I suppose, to other things. You can't go into management, then into engineering but you can do it the other way round.

Interviewer:	What was it that attracted you, particularly, to mechanical engineering and say not civil or electrical or aeronautical?

Subject:	Do you know I'd applied for aero (uh huh) for my foundation year and I didn't get offered that – I got offered mech eng instead. But I think it's a bit diverse. Again, you can come into whatever discipline you choose afterwards. It's not as specific as say aero where you couldn't then move into civils, things like that.

Interviewer:	OK, are you doing the sandwich course?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	OK. And, how did you decide to do that and why did you decide? 

Subject:	I thought it would be a good opportunity to learn what it's about, whether it's what I want to do (yeah) or whether it isn't. Yeah, just to get a feel for it, I think.

Interviewer:	OK, how did you decide to study at [this] University?

Subject:	Er, I travelled to a couple of universities, seeing what they had to offer (yeah) erm [university] actually offered me a better – well, not so much a better degree but offered me what I wanted – the aeronautical – but, having been round them all I kind of felt that [this university] felt (yeah) felt right. It's where I should be. You know you get the feelings some time that this is right and I fit in here, so.

Interviewer:	OK. When you decided that you were interested in engineering did you realise that it was so male dominated?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Did that bother you at all?

Subject:	No, not really.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that more women should be encouraged into engineering?

Subject:	Yeah, but I don't think it's the encouragement that they need, it's a change in the teaching practise. I think all girls and boys learn differently and the way in which you're taught (yeah) in engineering subjects suits boys far more than it does suit girls and I think (OK) I think sort of saying, oh girls you can do engineering is actually gonna benefit, it's going to increase the numbers – it needs to change.

Interviewer:	OK, what, if anything, would encourage or discourage you from doing engineering?

Subject:	I think something that changed my mind was, when I was about 17 er one of my DT teachers asked us whether I wanted to do this airspace challenge competition and it was a design project to re-design one of the RAF's fast jets. And, bringing in projects like that, when you're that sort of age, sort of GCSE/A levels, gives you an insight into what – what you could be doing and what – and I think that helped, whereas I mean, at the moment, or it least it has been for the past 2 or 3 years now, it's all maths, physics, maths, physics – it's really boring (laughter) but bringing in some kind of project – even though that was a bit outrageous, something to focus what you're doing on would help.

Interviewer:	OK, what characteristics do you think make a good engineer? How would you describe like an ideal engineer?

Subject:	Oh, erm open-minded, willing to listen to other people's ideas. Probably a good, a good leader, but team work is a big part of it.

Interviewer:	Do you think any of those characteristics are particularly male characteristics or female characteristics?

Subject:	Not really, I think it probably suits females more. (Yeah?) Yeah, the team working and the open to all ideas, but just, if it's men that are doing it …

Interviewer:	Do you think there are advantages or disadvantages of being a woman in engineering?

Subject:	Yeah, I mean there always is, isn't there? Er, I've been told that if I get this RAF placement then the advantage of being a woman project engineer would be that all of the ground crew would ask for you to be their supervisor, if they went travelling abroad, so that's good. (laughter) There again but er disadvantages – I suppose what – the fact that it's mainly a male – there's mainly men involved, you know – get a bit of grief from them maybe, you know. A little bit of – well you know.

Interviewer:	Does that bother you?

Subject:	No, I don't think so.

Interviewer:	OK, what did you expect that the degree would be – like in terms of the gender proportions, or the type of skills that you're learning, or the type of teaching? Is it what you expected it to be?

Subject:	Erm, the male to female ratio was what I was expecting but I thought by now I'd have some sort of more hands on, you know, I think. Like I went to the motor club the other week, to watch a couple of my friends taking out an engine. And I'm like oh, while I'm doing all these things about engines and systems, I couldn't tell you what these things were, and I think that probably affects what I can do, in terms of industry – like if you've got a part and it needs to be supervised, taken out or whatever, and you don't even know what it looks like, how it works, all you've got is a triangle on a piece of paper and the guys there, obviously knew, it'd probably be detrimental. So probably a bit more hands on, more examples – realistic examples.

Interviewer:	OK what's been the best and worst things about the course so far?

Subject:	The best bits have probably been the design projects (yeah) – realistic problems that need solving, but, at the same time, working in the teams for these projects has probably been the worst part. You know, trying to get people, especially the boys, to listen to anything that you're saying is difficult, even though they're the best part of the course.

Interviewer:	Yeah, and do you have to do much group work?

Subject:	Yeah. There's been quite a bit this year – last year wasn't so much but …

Interviewer:	When you're doing group work how do you decide who you're going to work with?

Subject:	Most of the time we get told (right) who we're working with. When we do get to choose, I tend to stick within the people I know I can work best with.

Interviewer:	Yeah, can they be males or females generally?

Subject:	One of the groups has been all guys that I chose to work with, and another one – another is – it was a girl – it doesn't really matter.

Interviewer:	OK what good and bad experiences have you had, working in groups?

Subject:	One that jumps to mind was a bad experience when there was me and this other girl – [name] – and then there was 2 boys. Erm, the project – it wasn't a project, it was a challenge, to drop an egg from fairly high and for it not to smash. So we had to make this parachute and design it and all the rest of it and there was a set number of things we could use, and costing it and stuff. The boys just wouldn't listen to a word that Rachel was saying, and what they were coming up with was complete rubbish (laughter) and I took on, sort of like, the leader of all them and I had to kind of persuade them to listen to what she was saying, and that I found really frustrating, that they just wouldn't listen. I think mainly because she was a girl (yeah) but it was just, oh we know how to do this, you know, we've done this sort of thing before. And, she had by far the best idea and once I got them to listen, we carried out that idea and it was alright, but trying to get them to do it, yeah.

Interviewer:	Ok, are you pleased that you chose to do this course?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Is it different to what you thought it would be? Did you think there would be more hands-on stuff?

Subject:	Yeah, I thought there would be more hands on stuff – more or maybe not so much hands on stuff but at least something to show us…

Interviewer:	Like using real life examples?

Subject:	Like all these forces we've discussed and talks and that, all you see is a line on an OHP and what – you don't actually see a beam with these weights and dampers and stuff, and I think being able to see what they're actually talking about – it would help.

Interviewer:	OK. Have you been taught by male and female lecturers?

Subject:	Yeah – one female but mainly male.

Interviewer:	OK, have you noticed any differences in their styles of teaching, for the males and females?

Subject:	Yes and no. I mean she was – the only one lecturer we've had wasn't well, when she taught us, seriously – erm, well not very well at all. And, she'd get schizo in the class and cry and stuff, which didn't make us that confident about going into engineering – but no, there wasn't really much difference in the way they taught. She was more approachable, but apart from that nothing really.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think you'd find it encouraging if you had more female lecturers?

Subject:	Yes. Er, you'd be able to think OK, right, if they can do it we can do it (yeah) and you can see that they've actually achieved something (yeah). Oh, I don't mind being like that.

Interviewer:	Have you got a personal tutor?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Are they male or female?

Subject:	Male.

Interviewer:	And have you had to go to them for anything?

Subject:	Er, well yeah, I've had to get a couple of references off him, but every time I go, he doesn't know who I am or what I'm here for. Nothing personal though.

Interviewer:	No, would you have rather had a female personal tutor?

Subject:	It doesn't really matter.

Interviewer:	Who or what do you think has been the biggest influence on you, since you started your degree?

Subject:	Phew, er, ooh, well we've had encouragement from a couple of the staff in particular (yeah) when you walk through the department they say hello, how you're doing? What are you up to? That kind of makes you want to, oh yes, I'll keep going, this is not too hard, stuff like that. There's been 1 or 2 individuals.

Interviewer:	OK, what aspects of the course do you think will help you on your placement?

Subject:	I think the ability to take a few steps back and think OK, what is the problem here? - is one that's been taught a lot, especially when it comes to the maths and physics, you can't just jump in there and know what the answer is. You've got to step by step go through what you've been given and what you can use and I think that system could work in any sort of environment, And I think moving into the placement environment, that would help being able to (yeah).

Interviewer:	So it's not just the actual technical side of things?

Subject:	Yeah, I can imagine a lot of the technical things won't be used but the general feeling of what goes on, steps to take would…

Interviewer:	OK, do you feel ready to go on placement? Do you feel prepared now (yeah) at this like particular time?

Subject:	I want to be there now, I don't want to be here any longer.

Interviewer:	Have university helped prepare you at all?

Subject:	Erm, [placement coordinator], the project, you know, the Careers woman, she's excellent at what she does. She's supportive, she – she lets you know what's going on, and from that side of things, yeah. Erm, we've had the odd careers talk and we've been made aware of what is available to us, if we want to use it.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think your educational experience and the way you're taught will reflect what it's really like in industry?

Subject:	No. I don't think so.

Interviewer:	OK, any particular reasons? Do you think it should be geared more so it is like the real world, or like the engineering industry?

Subject:	Yeah, I think so, but that would probably make what you do a lot narrower (yeah) and it would then end up being like another aero course where, what you do is so structured that you can't then progress onto anything else.

Interviewer:	OK, why did you decide to go on placement?

Subject:	Well, like I said before, just the opportunity to get a feel of what – whether engineering was for me.

Interviewer:	OK, did anyone particularly encourage you or discourage you from going on a placement?

Subject:	I think, speaking to a lot of my friends, they all said it was worthwhile (yeah) and the year they always – they thought was a very good year when – where they sort of grew up and it also gave them links and people speak to you afterwards – potential employers and stuff like that.

Interviewer:	OK, do you know where you're going yet – on placement?

Subject:	No, I've been offered a few places but none of them have been what I applied for initially.

Interviewer:	OK, so you're still …

Subject:	So I'm still undecided yet.

Interviewer:	OK, the places that you've applied to, how did you decide to apply to those companies?

Subject:	Do you mean in terms of why did I do it, or..?

Interviewer:	Yeah, like did you have criteria of what you wanted to be doing and those companies met those criteria - as in either the type of work, or the money that they were offering or training opportunities?

Subject:	Yeah, the main thing was erm interest – whether it was going to be interesting or not (yeah) and my interests have been, since I was quite young, have been sort of the defence industry – planes, erm tanks, things like that. So I went for them mainly. However, I have applied for other ones that I thought could be interesting, could be worth going for, and sort of like [company] er I can't think of any others at the moment, but yeah, I've done [company], [company], the RAF, and maybe 3 or 4 others.

Interviewer:	OK. Have what you've applied for and what you've been offered been quite different really?

Subject:	Yeah. I don't know whether you'll find this interesting or not but I've gone for engineering positions and they've offered like a safety role or a production management role and they all seem to be saying oh yeah, you're doing alright, we're interested in you but not for the engineering roles, why not do something – well, it sounds a bit bad – but more female orientated, you know.

Interviewer:	Yeah, do you feel like that is the reason they've offered you them roles?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah.

Interviewer:	That's quite interesting. ( yes, like) If you wanted to do them jobs you wouldn't be doing an engineering degree

Subject:	Well, they'd say like, oh well the safety role will involve some engineering but that's not what I applied for. And production and manufacturing or management – oh yeah, that would involve engineering as well but I think the point is that they're not offering us the engineering placements. They're bringing up something new.

Interviewer:	Are you still waiting to hear from some other people then?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, did you do much research into the companies that you applied for?

Subject:	Yeah – mainly web site stuff though. I think most of the information that we needed was on their web sites. Some of them, the web sites were quite good.

Interviewer:	Were the university very involved in helping you find the placement or apply to them?

Subject:	Yeah, [placement coordinator] sends us emails out, hundreds of them a week. Yeah, she's very good at that and she normally explains what they're looking for and how to apply. And most of them are on-line now, so we just go away and do it. Er like I went to the Careers Service to – Careers Centre to find out some information on [company] that I couldn't find elsewhere.

Interviewer:	Did you ever consider getting sponsored? 

Subject:	Sort of by the company? (Yeah) Like at the end, or before?

Interviewer:	At the start of your course – I think a few people – I don't know on the mechanical so much, but I know a few people, particularly doing civil engineering, are sponsored from the start of the course, and then they go on a placement year with them and they've probably got a job with them at the end.

Subject:	Yeah. I suppose I thought – that I think that I'm not 100% sure that this is what I want to do and signing on the dotted line meant that you would end up feeling cornered.

Interviewer:	OK, you've probably touched on this already, but what are the things that you're expecting to get out of your placement? Other than putting the theory into practice. You've said you've found something quite – it's helped you like grow up, so is that the type of thing that you're looking for as well?

Subject:	Yeah. Er, a bit of confidence, a bit more – you know – people skills and opportunities after the year.

Interviewer:	Do you think it will improve your career prospects at the end (yeah) when you're applying for a job?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah.

Interviewer:	What do you think will be the worst and best things about being on placement?

Subject:	I think it'll be fun. I think if I can – so long as it's semi-interesting, I can normally enjoy what I'm doing, so I think that'll be good. And probably the worst bit'll be the banter from the – from the shop floormen or whatever it'll be, but hopefully that won't be bad banter it'll be (you think you can cope with it?) – an acceptable level, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, how do you expect the work to differ from university?

Subject:	I think it'll be more get up and speak to people or go find out what's going on. More management – people management.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the skills you'll be using will be different?

Subject:	Erm, I don't know – on our course it's a lot of maths and physics. Very little is report writing, but I imagine in the industrial placement it'll all have swapped and that the report writing will take on a much bigger – bigger part of what you're doing and the maths be – sort of you leave the computer to do that or you get somebody else to do it. You know, I don't think that'll take on as much as it does at the moment.

Interviewer:	Are you looking forward to it, doing more report writing and that, or aren't you bothered?

Subject:	Yeah. I don't like number crunching so much, so yeah, I suppose so.

Interviewer:	OK, in terms of your career, where do you see yourself in 5 years time?

Subject:	Hmm, I don't know. Crocodile farm, I don't know (laughter). I think probably – I'm hoping to go into the RAF but we'll see after this industrial year whether or not, you know, it's – I'm suited to it, if I get it that is. (Yeah) And I think probably I'd move into a more people management position within that. I don't think I'd be a very good stress engineer, or fatigue or anything really engineering (yeah) you know. I think it'd be project management.

Interviewer:	OK, so in the longer term – sort of say 10 years time, do you think you'll be in the same industry?

Subject:	Hmm – yeah – yeah, but probably moving into I don't know into the ergonomics or human factors or something like that (yeah) rather than heavy engineering probably something more managerial.

Interviewer:	OK, you've said that you really want to go and work in the RAF so how would you describe your ideal career?

Subject:	Ooh – travel, opportunities to change what you're doing (yeah), security – I think it's a big thing with that one. Er, I suppose flexibility within the company to change.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that you'll find any difficulties in finding that ideal career?

Subject:	Yeah (laugher) erm, yeah, you've just got to give and take a bit haven't you? (Yeah) I'm not in it for the money, I just want to enjoy what I'm doing. I don't understand these people that do a job that they hate, just for the money that you can get. So, as long as it's stimulating in some kind of way.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that your career prospects are good and your field of entering?

Subject:	I think at the moment they are yeah, because of - they seem to be seriously lacking in engineers so the – they seem to be opening up new ideas, new doors, giving you more opportunity to do what you want to do, just to get you on board. So I think yeah, the opportunities that exist at the moment are very good although there's a lot of manufacturing and stuff going abroad.

Interviewer:	Yeah, and would you like to go and work abroad?

Subject:	Yeah, but probably not to China or the places that it's moving to. Oh, I wouldn't mind it for 6 months, a year or something like that, but not long term.

Interviewer:	OK, are you happy with all the career choices that you've made so far?

Subject:	I think so. They may not be the right ones but I don't think they can be the wrong ones.

Interviewer:	If you had to go through it all again, would you do anything differently?

Subject:	No, I don't think so. I thought for a while, that taking the A levels that I did was a bad idea, but I've found since like er just being able to get through the computer assessment (yeah) of like what grades did you get? Oh, 2 A's and a B, you know even though they may be in completely random subjects, has been better, and taking the foundation year (yeah). It's meant I've had time at university where I can enjoy myself than trying to do physics and maths at A level which I wouldn't have been able to do (yeah, so it hasn't hindered you at all). There was no sort of people at school that did physics and maths or anything like that so it would have been completely impossible and then – the rubbish grades, you know, if you came out with D's and E's, you wouldn't even get through the computer assessment, which I'm finding a lot of my friends are struggling with at the moment.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you're better off then in some ways than other people on the course because you've done a foundation year?

Subject:	Yeah, far better. Just the whole first year, whereas I'd been here a year, I knew I was going on and I knew who to speak to – I was already settled in whereas these people were coming in, straight from school, onto a degree course which was very intense and they had to try and settle in as well. (yeah) You know I was – I was doing alright like.

Interviewer:	OK, if you had to describe the culture and the characteristics of the engineering industry, how would you describe it in 5 words?

Subject:	Say that again.

Interviewer:	How would you describe the culture and characteristics of the engineering industry?

Subject:	 (Long pause) a bit technical, very male orientated, er yeah, I think that's about it.

Interviewer:	Why do you think it is so male orientated?

Subject:	I think just cos of traditions, and like I said before, the way it's taught but it's been men for centuries (yeah) and the whole schooling system means that men come out at the end of it.

Interviewer:	What do you think they can do to change that? Do you think they should change it?

Subject:	Yeah. But I think it's – it's got to be more social. A social change needs to happen (yeah) and I think that maybe that does start with school, I'm not sure. Yeah, at the lower levels it should be alright for girls to play with technic lego and get involved in technical things, whereas even as a kid, you felt like oh, I shouldn't be doing that – I shouldn't be taking my bike apart, I shouldn't be – you know – watching my dad playing with a car (yeah). It's - but I don't why that exists, am not sure – it definitely needs to start at school.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that any aspect of the engineering culture will be problematic for you?

Subject:	I think that what we've discussed before, what the components look like and being able to work out how that relates that to all the stuff we've done here. Is that what you mean, you know?

Interviewer:	Do you think the fact that you are a female in a male industry, will hold you back at all? Not through want of trying but from other people's attitudes?

Subject:	Yeah. It's gonna have some effect. I don't know how big an effect that would be, especially when you're into more management side of things. It takes it away. I mean if I wanted to be an engineer, an engineer – you know then I think that would be more affected than it would be if I wanted to move into management.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think your educational experiences differ, as an engineering student, from say social science students?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	How?

Subject:	We do a lot more hours than they do.

Interviewer:	Do you think that's a good thing?

Subject:	Er, it's more structured and I think if – when we go into industry or wherever you go to work, having that get up at half past seven to be there at nine o'clock, for lectures, erm it must help an awful lot. I mean I can imagine getting up for 10 o'clock, or you know, 2 o'clock geography sessions, wouldn't get you into that kind of mind – mind frame. But I (it doesn't, I can tell you that from experience) that must help and having a structure to your day must help. I think they must get other things out of it as well. Socially I think they're much better. I don't know – dealing with social sciences but they seem to communicate better, talk to people better (yeah) whereas, 'cos we're sitting, listening to somebody for 5/6 hours a day, you don't get to talk much.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the group work that you do helps that communication side of things?

Subject:	Yeah, but – oh yeah, I suppose it does but not to the same extent that they can – I'm sure they must do discussion sessions and a lot more of that. I suppose, even in our tutorials it's sit there and listen. It's listening the whole time. Yet, like I've not heard say more than 50% of my course speak, so you know if they speak, I'm like, oh, that's what they sound like - I'm sure that doesn't happen down in Social Science but…

Interviewer:	Do you think that's 'cos there's more men?

Subject:	Probably.

Interviewer:	And women just generally talk more.

Subject:	Yes. (laughter)

Interviewer:	Ok, that's it really, thank you very much.

turns.text: Er, I've done a couple of summer jobs erm but for 3 years I was a gymnastics coach for (??) but nothing in terms of engineering (right, OK) I've done the odd week here and there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Right, OK – what do your parents do? Are they engineers or anything?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, my dad's a Financial Manager and my mum's a Nurse.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, I'm just going to ask you then a bit about why and how you decided to do engineering. So, what do you think made you decide to go into engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don't know. I wanted to join the air force and then applied to be a pilot (right) and I was too short and I thought well if you can't – if you can't fly them, why not learn how they work and how to design them or how to build them you know, and it ended up carrying on from that really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Right, OK, so in terms of things that influenced your decision, it was probably the type of job that you wanted to do, or that you weren't able to do – ended up leading you into it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, as a kid I always sort of played with technic lego and stuff like that. And my Design, Technology I enjoyed and I got good marks and – and it carried on from there really, along with a couple of other things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Have you come straight from school to University?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I did a foundation year, here at [this university].

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, so what about things like your family and careers advice, anything like that? Did that help you or…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Careers Advice was awful at the school.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Was it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, there wasn't really a lot of that, and what there was it was like, oh well how do you fancy becoming – you know – a shop assistant or erm, or what was I told I should become? – a shop fitter, you know. Putting shelves up in a shop basically – that was about as much information they gave and it was awful. You saw a Careers Advice person for say maybe, for 20 minutes, once a year, and it was a waste of time. (yeah) A complete waste of time.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you tell them what you wanted to do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And what kind of reaction did that get?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It was nothing really and…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And what about your family, have they been supportive?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, they're supportive of whatever I chose to do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah? OK, did you know any engineers to talk to, to find out what it is all about?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I have a very close family friend who is just a retired – retired chartered engineer (right) and he kind of gave us some advice, told us a lot about the fact that our course is a lot of mathematical stuff, and in the end you just put it into a computer and it's part of what – of what – a lot of what you do here is not what you do in industry. (Yeah) But, not an awful lot of people really, just the odd one or two.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, but what your friend said didn't put you off at all? What are the sorts of things that appeal to you about doing engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, working on technical projects and I think the engineering side of things moves more into management as you progress. And I think project management and that kind of thing. Also, I'd always thought about being some sort of human factors – er, you know, the way people interact with machines or stuff – or ergonomics always interested me. It kind of opens doors I suppose, to other things. You can't go into management, then into engineering but you can do it the other way round.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What was it that attracted you, particularly, to mechanical engineering and say not civil or electrical or aeronautical?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Do you know I'd applied for aero (uh huh) for my foundation year and I didn't get offered that – I got offered mech eng instead. But I think it's a bit diverse. Again, you can come into whatever discipline you choose afterwards. It's not as specific as say aero where you couldn't then move into civils, things like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are you doing the sandwich course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. And, how did you decide to do that and why did you decide?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I thought it would be a good opportunity to learn what it's about, whether it's what I want to do (yeah) or whether it isn't. Yeah, just to get a feel for it, I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how did you decide to study at [this] University?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I travelled to a couple of universities, seeing what they had to offer (yeah) erm [university] actually offered me a better – well, not so much a better degree but offered me what I wanted – the aeronautical – but, having been round them all I kind of felt that [this university] felt (yeah) felt right. It's where I should be. You know you get the feelings some time that this is right and I fit in here, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. When you decided that you were interested in engineering did you realise that it was so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did that bother you at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that more women should be encouraged into engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, but I don't think it's the encouragement that they need, it's a change in the teaching practise. I think all girls and boys learn differently and the way in which you're taught (yeah) in engineering subjects suits boys far more than it does suit girls and I think (OK) I think sort of saying, oh girls you can do engineering is actually gonna benefit, it's going to increase the numbers – it needs to change.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what, if anything, would encourage or discourage you from doing engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think something that changed my mind was, when I was about 17 er one of my DT teachers asked us whether I wanted to do this airspace challenge competition and it was a design project to re-design one of the RAF's fast jets. And, bringing in projects like that, when you're that sort of age, sort of GCSE/A levels, gives you an insight into what – what you could be doing and what – and I think that helped, whereas I mean, at the moment, or it least it has been for the past 2 or 3 years now, it's all maths, physics, maths, physics – it's really boring (laughter) but bringing in some kind of project – even though that was a bit outrageous, something to focus what you're doing on would help.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what characteristics do you think make a good engineer? How would you describe like an ideal engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh, erm open-minded, willing to listen to other people's ideas. Probably a good, a good leader, but team work is a big part of it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think any of those characteristics are particularly male characteristics or female characteristics?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really, I think it probably suits females more. (Yeah?) Yeah, the team working and the open to all ideas, but just, if it's men that are doing it …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think there are advantages or disadvantages of being a woman in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I mean there always is, isn't there? Er, I've been told that if I get this RAF placement then the advantage of being a woman project engineer would be that all of the ground crew would ask for you to be their supervisor, if they went travelling abroad, so that's good. (laughter) There again but er disadvantages – I suppose what – the fact that it's mainly a male – there's mainly men involved, you know – get a bit of grief from them maybe, you know. A little bit of – well you know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Does that bother you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I don't think so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what did you expect that the degree would be – like in terms of the gender proportions, or the type of skills that you're learning, or the type of teaching? Is it what you expected it to be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, the male to female ratio was what I was expecting but I thought by now I'd have some sort of more hands on, you know, I think. Like I went to the motor club the other week, to watch a couple of my friends taking out an engine. And I'm like oh, while I'm doing all these things about engines and systems, I couldn't tell you what these things were, and I think that probably affects what I can do, in terms of industry – like if you've got a part and it needs to be supervised, taken out or whatever, and you don't even know what it looks like, how it works, all you've got is a triangle on a piece of paper and the guys there, obviously knew, it'd probably be detrimental. So probably a bit more hands on, more examples – realistic examples.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK what's been the best and worst things about the course so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The best bits have probably been the design projects (yeah) – realistic problems that need solving, but, at the same time, working in the teams for these projects has probably been the worst part. You know, trying to get people, especially the boys, to listen to anything that you're saying is difficult, even though they're the best part of the course.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, and do you have to do much group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. There's been quite a bit this year – last year wasn't so much but …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you're doing group work how do you decide who you're going to work with?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Most of the time we get told (right) who we're working with. When we do get to choose, I tend to stick within the people I know I can work best with.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, can they be males or females generally?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: One of the groups has been all guys that I chose to work with, and another one – another is – it was a girl – it doesn't really matter.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK what good and bad experiences have you had, working in groups?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: One that jumps to mind was a bad experience when there was me and this other girl – [name] – and then there was 2 boys. Erm, the project – it wasn't a project, it was a challenge, to drop an egg from fairly high and for it not to smash. So we had to make this parachute and design it and all the rest of it and there was a set number of things we could use, and costing it and stuff. The boys just wouldn't listen to a word that Rachel was saying, and what they were coming up with was complete rubbish (laughter) and I took on, sort of like, the leader of all them and I had to kind of persuade them to listen to what she was saying, and that I found really frustrating, that they just wouldn't listen. I think mainly because she was a girl (yeah) but it was just, oh we know how to do this, you know, we've done this sort of thing before. And, she had by far the best idea and once I got them to listen, we carried out that idea and it was alright, but trying to get them to do it, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, are you pleased that you chose to do this course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is it different to what you thought it would be? Did you think there would be more hands-on stuff?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I thought there would be more hands on stuff – more or maybe not so much hands on stuff but at least something to show us…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Like using real life examples?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Like all these forces we've discussed and talks and that, all you see is a line on an OHP and what – you don't actually see a beam with these weights and dampers and stuff, and I think being able to see what they're actually talking about – it would help.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Have you been taught by male and female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah – one female but mainly male.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you noticed any differences in their styles of teaching, for the males and females?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes and no. I mean she was – the only one lecturer we've had wasn't well, when she taught us, seriously – erm, well not very well at all. And, she'd get schizo in the class and cry and stuff, which didn't make us that confident about going into engineering – but no, there wasn't really much difference in the way they taught. She was more approachable, but apart from that nothing really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think you'd find it encouraging if you had more female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. Er, you'd be able to think OK, right, if they can do it we can do it (yeah) and you can see that they've actually achieved something (yeah). Oh, I don't mind being like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you got a personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are they male or female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Male.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And have you had to go to them for anything?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, well yeah, I've had to get a couple of references off him, but every time I go, he doesn't know who I am or what I'm here for. Nothing personal though.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: No, would you have rather had a female personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It doesn't really matter.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Who or what do you think has been the biggest influence on you, since you started your degree?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Phew, er, ooh, well we've had encouragement from a couple of the staff in particular (yeah) when you walk through the department they say hello, how you're doing? What are you up to? That kind of makes you want to, oh yes, I'll keep going, this is not too hard, stuff like that. There's been 1 or 2 individuals.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what aspects of the course do you think will help you on your placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think the ability to take a few steps back and think OK, what is the problem here? - is one that's been taught a lot, especially when it comes to the maths and physics, you can't just jump in there and know what the answer is. You've got to step by step go through what you've been given and what you can use and I think that system could work in any sort of environment, And I think moving into the placement environment, that would help being able to (yeah).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So it's not just the actual technical side of things?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I can imagine a lot of the technical things won't be used but the general feeling of what goes on, steps to take would…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you feel ready to go on placement? Do you feel prepared now (yeah) at this like particular time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I want to be there now, I don't want to be here any longer.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have university helped prepare you at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, [placement coordinator], the project, you know, the Careers woman, she's excellent at what she does. She's supportive, she – she lets you know what's going on, and from that side of things, yeah. Erm, we've had the odd careers talk and we've been made aware of what is available to us, if we want to use it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think your educational experience and the way you're taught will reflect what it's really like in industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. I don't think so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, any particular reasons? Do you think it should be geared more so it is like the real world, or like the engineering industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think so, but that would probably make what you do a lot narrower (yeah) and it would then end up being like another aero course where, what you do is so structured that you can't then progress onto anything else.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, why did you decide to go on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, like I said before, just the opportunity to get a feel of what – whether engineering was for me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did anyone particularly encourage you or discourage you from going on a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think, speaking to a lot of my friends, they all said it was worthwhile (yeah) and the year they always – they thought was a very good year when – where they sort of grew up and it also gave them links and people speak to you afterwards – potential employers and stuff like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you know where you're going yet – on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I've been offered a few places but none of them have been what I applied for initially.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, so you're still …

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: So I'm still undecided yet.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, the places that you've applied to, how did you decide to apply to those companies?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Do you mean in terms of why did I do it, or..?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, like did you have criteria of what you wanted to be doing and those companies met those criteria - as in either the type of work, or the money that they were offering or training opportunities?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, the main thing was erm interest – whether it was going to be interesting or not (yeah) and my interests have been, since I was quite young, have been sort of the defence industry – planes, erm tanks, things like that. So I went for them mainly. However, I have applied for other ones that I thought could be interesting, could be worth going for, and sort of like [company] er I can't think of any others at the moment, but yeah, I've done [company], [company], the RAF, and maybe 3 or 4 others.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Have what you've applied for and what you've been offered been quite different really?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I don't know whether you'll find this interesting or not but I've gone for engineering positions and they've offered like a safety role or a production management role and they all seem to be saying oh yeah, you're doing alright, we're interested in you but not for the engineering roles, why not do something – well, it sounds a bit bad – but more female orientated, you know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, do you feel like that is the reason they've offered you them roles?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That's quite interesting. ( yes, like) If you wanted to do them jobs you wouldn't be doing an engineering degree

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, they'd say like, oh well the safety role will involve some engineering but that's not what I applied for. And production and manufacturing or management – oh yeah, that would involve engineering as well but I think the point is that they're not offering us the engineering placements. They're bringing up something new.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you still waiting to hear from some other people then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you do much research into the companies that you applied for?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah – mainly web site stuff though. I think most of the information that we needed was on their web sites. Some of them, the web sites were quite good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Were the university very involved in helping you find the placement or apply to them?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, [placement coordinator] sends us emails out, hundreds of them a week. Yeah, she's very good at that and she normally explains what they're looking for and how to apply. And most of them are on-line now, so we just go away and do it. Er like I went to the Careers Service to – Careers Centre to find out some information on [company] that I couldn't find elsewhere.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you ever consider getting sponsored?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Sort of by the company? (Yeah) Like at the end, or before?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: At the start of your course – I think a few people – I don't know on the mechanical so much, but I know a few people, particularly doing civil engineering, are sponsored from the start of the course, and then they go on a placement year with them and they've probably got a job with them at the end.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I suppose I thought – that I think that I'm not 100% sure that this is what I want to do and signing on the dotted line meant that you would end up feeling cornered.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, you've probably touched on this already, but what are the things that you're expecting to get out of your placement? Other than putting the theory into practice. You've said you've found something quite – it's helped you like grow up, so is that the type of thing that you're looking for as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. Er, a bit of confidence, a bit more – you know – people skills and opportunities after the year.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it will improve your career prospects at the end (yeah) when you're applying for a job?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think will be the worst and best things about being on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it'll be fun. I think if I can – so long as it's semi-interesting, I can normally enjoy what I'm doing, so I think that'll be good. And probably the worst bit'll be the banter from the – from the shop floormen or whatever it'll be, but hopefully that won't be bad banter it'll be (you think you can cope with it?) – an acceptable level, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how do you expect the work to differ from university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it'll be more get up and speak to people or go find out what's going on. More management – people management.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the skills you'll be using will be different?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don't know – on our course it's a lot of maths and physics. Very little is report writing, but I imagine in the industrial placement it'll all have swapped and that the report writing will take on a much bigger – bigger part of what you're doing and the maths be – sort of you leave the computer to do that or you get somebody else to do it. You know, I don't think that'll take on as much as it does at the moment.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you looking forward to it, doing more report writing and that, or aren't you bothered?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I don't like number crunching so much, so yeah, I suppose so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, in terms of your career, where do you see yourself in 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm, I don't know. Crocodile farm, I don't know (laughter). I think probably – I'm hoping to go into the RAF but we'll see after this industrial year whether or not, you know, it's – I'm suited to it, if I get it that is. (Yeah) And I think probably I'd move into a more people management position within that. I don't think I'd be a very good stress engineer, or fatigue or anything really engineering (yeah) you know. I think it'd be project management.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, so in the longer term – sort of say 10 years time, do you think you'll be in the same industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm – yeah – yeah, but probably moving into I don't know into the ergonomics or human factors or something like that (yeah) rather than heavy engineering probably something more managerial.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, you've said that you really want to go and work in the RAF so how would you describe your ideal career?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Ooh – travel, opportunities to change what you're doing (yeah), security – I think it's a big thing with that one. Er, I suppose flexibility within the company to change.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that you'll find any difficulties in finding that ideal career?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah (laugher) erm, yeah, you've just got to give and take a bit haven't you? (Yeah) I'm not in it for the money, I just want to enjoy what I'm doing. I don't understand these people that do a job that they hate, just for the money that you can get. So, as long as it's stimulating in some kind of way.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that your career prospects are good and your field of entering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think at the moment they are yeah, because of - they seem to be seriously lacking in engineers so the – they seem to be opening up new ideas, new doors, giving you more opportunity to do what you want to do, just to get you on board. So I think yeah, the opportunities that exist at the moment are very good although there's a lot of manufacturing and stuff going abroad.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, and would you like to go and work abroad?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, but probably not to China or the places that it's moving to. Oh, I wouldn't mind it for 6 months, a year or something like that, but not long term.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are you happy with all the career choices that you've made so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so. They may not be the right ones but I don't think they can be the wrong ones.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: If you had to go through it all again, would you do anything differently?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I don't think so. I thought for a while, that taking the A levels that I did was a bad idea, but I've found since like er just being able to get through the computer assessment (yeah) of like what grades did you get? Oh, 2 A's and a B, you know even though they may be in completely random subjects, has been better, and taking the foundation year (yeah). It's meant I've had time at university where I can enjoy myself than trying to do physics and maths at A level which I wouldn't have been able to do (yeah, so it hasn't hindered you at all). There was no sort of people at school that did physics and maths or anything like that so it would have been completely impossible and then – the rubbish grades, you know, if you came out with D's and E's, you wouldn't even get through the computer assessment, which I'm finding a lot of my friends are struggling with at the moment.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you're better off then in some ways than other people on the course because you've done a foundation year?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, far better. Just the whole first year, whereas I'd been here a year, I knew I was going on and I knew who to speak to – I was already settled in whereas these people were coming in, straight from school, onto a degree course which was very intense and they had to try and settle in as well. (yeah) You know I was – I was doing alright like.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, if you had to describe the culture and the characteristics of the engineering industry, how would you describe it in 5 words?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Say that again.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How would you describe the culture and characteristics of the engineering industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: (Long pause) a bit technical, very male orientated, er yeah, I think that's about it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think it is so male orientated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think just cos of traditions, and like I said before, the way it's taught but it's been men for centuries (yeah) and the whole schooling system means that men come out at the end of it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think they can do to change that? Do you think they should change it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. But I think it's – it's got to be more social. A social change needs to happen (yeah) and I think that maybe that does start with school, I'm not sure. Yeah, at the lower levels it should be alright for girls to play with technic lego and get involved in technical things, whereas even as a kid, you felt like oh, I shouldn't be doing that – I shouldn't be taking my bike apart, I shouldn't be – you know – watching my dad playing with a car (yeah). It's - but I don't why that exists, am not sure – it definitely needs to start at school.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that any aspect of the engineering culture will be problematic for you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think that what we've discussed before, what the components look like and being able to work out how that relates that to all the stuff we've done here. Is that what you mean, you know?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think the fact that you are a female in a male industry, will hold you back at all? Not through want of trying but from other people's attitudes?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. It's gonna have some effect. I don't know how big an effect that would be, especially when you're into more management side of things. It takes it away. I mean if I wanted to be an engineer, an engineer – you know then I think that would be more affected than it would be if I wanted to move into management.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think your educational experiences differ, as an engineering student, from say social science students?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: We do a lot more hours than they do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that's a good thing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, it's more structured and I think if – when we go into industry or wherever you go to work, having that get up at half past seven to be there at nine o'clock, for lectures, erm it must help an awful lot. I mean I can imagine getting up for 10 o'clock, or you know, 2 o'clock geography sessions, wouldn't get you into that kind of mind – mind frame. But I (it doesn't, I can tell you that from experience) that must help and having a structure to your day must help. I think they must get other things out of it as well. Socially I think they're much better. I don't know – dealing with social sciences but they seem to communicate better, talk to people better (yeah) whereas, 'cos we're sitting, listening to somebody for 5/6 hours a day, you don't get to talk much.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the group work that you do helps that communication side of things?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, but – oh yeah, I suppose it does but not to the same extent that they can – I'm sure they must do discussion sessions and a lot more of that. I suppose, even in our tutorials it's sit there and listen. It's listening the whole time. Yet, like I've not heard say more than 50% of my course speak, so you know if they speak, I'm like, oh, that's what they sound like - I'm sure that doesn't happen down in Social Science but…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that's 'cos there's more men?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Probably.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And women just generally talk more.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. (laughter)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, that's it really, thank you very much.
